#### First Sequence: Tuscan Utterance
Signor Baroncini was instructed to ascend to the rock platform known as the *Pulpit West* and pronounce three times, at an initial intensity of ninety decibels (calibrated by the deflection of the Koenig manometric capsule at two metres distance), the test noun:

$$\text{Test Noun A: } \textbf{SOLITUDINE} \quad \text{[/so.li'tu.di.ne/]}$$

*Observations:*  
The vowels */o/* and */u/*—characterized by standard Italian formant distributions at $F_1 = 450\text{ Hz}$, $F_2 = 800\text{ Hz}$—suffered immediate and catastrophic destructive interference.

Upon leaving the speaker’s mouth, the acoustic wave struck the vertical fluting of the eastern wall (a series of organ-pipe stalagmites known locally as *The Twelve Apostles*). The high liquid dental consonant */t/* was scattered by the rough micro-facets of the limestone; the final vowel */e/* dropped below the threshold of legal legibility ($0.12\text{ dynes/cm}^2$) at a distance of merely eighty-six metres from the point of vocalization.

Baroncini shouted that the air currents from the lower canyon were skewing the results; his spittle, bright and white in the acetylene light, landed upon the brass rim of the sound-funnel.

"The cavern is damp!" he cried. "The humidity creates an artificial viscosity! No civilized language was meant to be spoken in a sewer!"

I informed him that under the Protocol of St. Germain, atmospheric variables cannot be excluded from cadastral computations unless the deviation exceeds three standard barometric atmospheres. He wiped his nose with a silk handkerchief that smelled of lavender and damp wool, then sat upon the instrument case, muttering.

#### Second Sequence: Kras Utterance
The Slovene guide, Hrovat, was positioned upon the corresponding platform (*Pulpit East*), sixty metres across the central void. He was instructed to deliver the phonetic equivalent:

$$\text{Test Noun B: } \textbf{SAMOTA} \quad \text{[/sa'mɔ:ta/]}$$

*Observations:*  
Hrovat did not stand erect. He leaned forward, his hands resting upon his knees, his jaw dropped in the manner of the Carniolan wood-cutters when they call across the timber-chutes.

The open vowel */a/* ($F_1 = 680\text{ Hz}$, $F_2 = 1050\text{ Hz}$), delivered with the deep, pharyngealized timbre characteristic of the lower Kras, entered into immediate acoustic coupling with the fundamental resonant mode of the chamber. The sound did not disperse; it appeared to gather the dampness of the walls into itself.

The nasal consonant */m/* acted as an impedance-matching transformer between his larynx and the air volume of the chasm:

The trace on the smoked glass cylinder did not decay. For 11.8 seconds after the termination of his vocal effort, the stylus continued to etch a clean, sinusoidal wave into the carbon layer. The limestone ceiling—scored with thousands of solution-pockets (*karren*)—acted not as an absorbent, but as a regenerative feedback grid.

The sound returned from the northern branch of the chasm not as a faint repetition, but as an amplified standing wave, vibrating through the cast-iron legs of the Marey chronograph with such force that the alcohol meniscus in the level-vial boiled into foam.

Under the letter of the Rapallo convention, this result extends the sovereign frontier of the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes three hundred and forty-four metres westward through the solid core of the plateau, cutting directly through the subterranean military water-conduit constructed by the Italian 3rd Army in 1917.

Baroncini stood up, his face yellow in the carbide glare.

"This is not grammar," he said, his voice dropping into that flat, dangerous quietness one hears in the military tribunals. "This is a deformity of the palate. The man is not speaking; he is vomiting a vowel which happens to fit the dimensions of a hole in the mud. If the League of Nations accepts that an ape’s grunt can move a military frontier, then we have fought eleven battles on the Isonzo for nothing."

He reached for the Marey cylinder, intending to wipe the lampblack with his thumb.

I placed my palm against his chest. His coat was cold and soaked through with the alkaline drippings from the vault. Beneath the broadcloth, his ribs were as thin and rigid as the stays of a corset.

"The stylus does not lie, Signor Baroncini," I said. "The record is fixed in the carbon."

"The carbon belongs to the State," he whispered.

Neither of us moved. Between us, Hrovat remained crouched on his ledge of rock, his lantern dark to save carbide, his silhouette indistinguishable from the stalagmites that rose around him like a petrified congregation.

Baroncini has climbed back to the intermediate station at -80 metres. He claims he has an inflammation of the pleura; he could not bear the sound of the water, which he swears contains a persistent, dry coughing like that of his brother who died of phosgene gas in the military hospital at Cividale.

Hrovat is gone. He vanished into the lower crawl-ways six hours ago with an unlit tallow dip between his teeth, searching for an air-pocket where the Kras dialect might cross the subterranean watershed into the Timavo springs.

I am alone in the lowest chamber of the system.

The lampblack on my remaining glass plates has become damp; it sloughs off the glass in greasy ribbons, like the skin from a boiled pear. I have discarded the chronograph clockwork. It is no longer necessary. The measurements can be taken directly through the gutta-percha tubes inserted into the auditory canal.

The river does not roar here. The water is forced through a horizontal fissure three inches high under hydraulic pressure so immense that the sound is converted into a continuous, dry rustling—a sound identical to that of five hundred women turning the pages of their prayer books simultaneously in a cold stone church.

I dipped the brass sound-collector into the black current at 01:20 hours.

The acoustic profile is not random. It does not conform to the Gaussian distribution of turbulent fluid flow.

When the signal is filtered through the 435 Hz resonator, the turbulent noise resolves into discrete phonetic clusters. They are not Italian. They are not Slovene. They are the collapsed, uninflected case-endings of the polyglot imperial regiments that held the trenches on Monte San Michele in the summer of 1916:

*...hier... hier... doli... vodo... gib acht... noch eins...*

They have been preserved in the limestone.

The mountain is a phonographic cylinder of seven hundred square miles. The calcium carbonate, dissolved by the acidic rain of twelve years ago—rain that fell through the smoke of two million high-explosive shells—has recrystallized upon the cavern walls as a porous, acoustic varnish.

Every shriek uttered into the mud of the Doberdò sinkholes has filtered down through the rock-sinks, drop by drop, grain by grain, carried by the seepage water into these lower cisterns where the air does not move.

The sound is not fading. It is accumulating.

> 
> If I mark the boundary according to the Koenig flame readings, the frontier will run directly through his larynx.
>

They would pave it with concrete; they would build an electric pumping station at the bottom; they would drown the voices in fifty thousand gallons of chlorated drinking water for the dockyards of Monfalcone.

The light is failing. The carbide has turned into a grey mush that smells of garlic and dead pond-water.

It is not an absence of light; it is a solid, heavy substance that presses against the eyeballs until the retina creates its own small, pale phosphorescences—little running figures that turn into Roman numerals, and then into cadastral benchmarks, and then into nothing.

I can hear the Marey chronograph needle scraping against the bare glass. The clockwork has run down, but the cylinder is still turning, driven by the vibrations of the river below.

It is not recording me.
